list_one.title: A 32-bit length taken off the socket sizes a byte array before any payload arrives, behind a cast guard that is not a limit
list_one.impact: A peer that can write to the socket — a hostile or compromised broker, or an on-path attacker on a connection without TLS — commits up to roughly 2 GB of client heap per decoded value by sending four bytes. The result is an OutOfMemoryError in the process that embeds this library, which is an availability failure of the consuming application rather than of the broker. Because the byte-vector and long-string types are legal inside a field table, the same trick can be repeated per table entry within one frame, so the peer does not need many round trips.

list_one.title: The peer chooses whether the decoder fails with a protocol exception or with an unchecked one, on a path declared to throw IOException
list_one.impact: A caller that closes the connection cleanly on IOException — the contract this method declares, and the one MalformedFrameException was written for — does not catch this. The peer can therefore steer the failure onto whatever generic handler sits above, which is at best a different shutdown path than the protocol-error one and at worst none, leaving the connection thread to die without the orderly close and listener notification the IOException path provides. The attacker gains a choice of failure mode on a client they were already able to disconnect, which is a small gain, not a new capability.

list_one.title: Mutual recursion between the field-value, table and array decoders carries no depth counter
list_one.impact: A peer that sends a deeply nested field table or field array drives the decoding thread into a StackOverflowError at a cost of a few bytes per stack frame. StackOverflowError is an Error, not an IOException, so it does not travel the path that MalformedFrameException (line 217) was written for: a caller that closes the connection cleanly on IOException will not catch it. The reachable outcome is the death of the connection's I/O thread, plus the per-level stream and map objects allocated on the way down. This is the neighbouring class WEB-26 names alongside the allocation in F-001, and both are reachable through the same readFieldValue switch.
list_one.evidence:
The cycle is closed inside this one file and no signature on it carries a depth parameter:
  line 158  static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)
  line 181      case 'F':  value = readTable(in);   // -> line 139 readTable
  line 184      case 'A':  value = readArray(in);   // -> line 237 readArray
  line 150      readTable:  Object value = readFieldValue(tableIn);
  line 245      readArray:  Object value = readFieldValue(arrayIn);
readTable is declared `private static Map<String,Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)` (line 139) and readArray `private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)` (line 237): neither takes a level argument, and no counter, ThreadLocal or configured maximum appears anywhere in the file. Each level of nesting costs the peer a handful of bytes — inside an array, one type byte 'A' plus a four-byte length is five bytes per frame of stack — while each level allocates a fresh TruncatedInputStream, a fresh DataInputStream and, for a table, a HashMap (lines 145-147, 241-243).

list_one.title: The timestamp decoder multiplies an attacker-chosen 64-bit value by 1000 with no overflow check
list_one.impact: An application that reads the AMQP timestamp property for ordering, expiry, deduplication or audit receives a Date the peer selected freely, including one far in the past or the future, from an encoded seconds value that looks unremarkable. Nothing is corrupted inside the library; the damage, if any, is in the consumer's use of the value. A peer that can set the timestamp field at all already influences it, so the extra capability is the ability to reach millisecond values that a non-wrapping conversion could not produce, and to do so without the encoded seconds looking anomalous to anything that inspects the frame.

list_one.title: The default build executes generator scripts over an external specification checkout that the manifest does not pin, and compiles the result into the published jar
list_one.impact: Whoever controls the contents of `deps/rabbitmq_codegen` on the machine that performs a release controls Java source that is compiled into the published library, with no signature or hash standing in the way. This is the shape SUP-04 exists for: the malicious content never has to appear in this repository's source tree, only in the build input, and the released jar carries it to every consumer. The same execution also runs a Groovy script and a Python script under the build's identity at generate-sources, so a compromise of either script file is code execution in the release environment.
list_one.evidence: The plugin is bound to the default lifecycle, not to a profile (pom.xml lines 595-638): goal `execute` at phase `generate-sources`, `<source>${groovy-scripts.dir}/generate_amqp_sources.groovy</source>`, with `<script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script>` and `<spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json</spec>`. The properties block resolves `${codegen.dir}` to `${basedir}/deps/rabbitmq_codegen` and documents it as "a working copy of rabbitmq-codegen"; `${codegen.spec_version}` is `0.9.1`, which pins the file name of the specification, not its content. build-helper-maven-plugin then adds `${project.build.directory}/generated-sources/src/main/java` to the compile roots (lines 640-658), so whatever those scripts emit is compiled into the artifact that maven-jar-plugin packages and central-publishing-maven-plugin publishes. Nowhere in the manifest is there a digest, a checksum verification, a signature check or a pinned revision for the contents of `${deps.dir}` — grep for `http://` returns only XML namespace declarations, so the risk here is not an unverified download inside the pom but an unverified working copy the pom consumes.

list_two.title: A repeated field name in a table is dropped silently, first occurrence wins
list_two.impact: Nothing on its own, and no exploit path is claimed here. It is recorded because duplicate-key handling is where header smuggling lives when two implementations disagree: a decoder that took the last occurrence would build a different map from the same bytes, and only one of the two would match what a signature, a broker-side filter or a second consumer saw.

list_two.title: A declared table or array length is never compared with the bytes that remain
list_two.impact: An over-declared length is not an error here, it is a licence to read further. A nested table or array that declares more bytes than its parent holds keeps consuming until the underlying stream ends, so it absorbs the sibling fields that followed it; the parent loop at line 148 then sees `available() == 0` and returns a map that silently lost them, with no MalformedFrameException raised. A decoder that validated the declared length against the enclosing region would reject the same frame. The result is a parser differential: this client and any stricter peer disagree about which headers a message carries, which matters wherever an application routes, filters, audits or authorizes on a header value.

list_two.title: The timestamp field multiplies a wire-chosen 64-bit value by 1000 unchecked
list_two.impact: The peer chooses which side of the epoch the decoded Date lands on, independently of the value it declared. Where a consumer compares that Date against now — message expiry, a deduplication or replay window, retention, ordering, an audit record — a wrapped value inverts the comparison, and the audit trail records a time the sender never sent.

list_two.title: Field tables and field arrays recurse with no depth counter anywhere in the chain
list_two.impact: A single frame of a few tens of kilobytes buys thousands of nesting levels, which is StackOverflowError in the thread decoding the frame. That is an Error, not an IOException: the `catch (IOException)` and MalformedFrameException handling the protocol layer is written around does not catch it, so the failure surfaces as a dead connection-reading thread rather than as a rejected frame. Each level also allocates a HashMap or ArrayList and two stream wrappers, so the same bytes buy a heap multiple on the way down.
list_two.evidence:
The cycle is closed and carries no depth argument in any of the three signatures:
  static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)            // line 158
      case 'F': value = readTable(in);                        // line 181
      case 'A': value = readArray(in);                        // line 184
  private static Map<String,Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)   // line 139
      while(tableIn.available() > 0) { readShortstr(tableIn); readFieldValue(tableIn); }   // lines 148-152
  private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)   // line 237
      while(arrayIn.available() > 0) { array.add(readFieldValue(arrayIn)); }               // lines 244-247
One nesting level costs the sender five bytes: the type tag 'F' or 'A' plus a four-byte length. Nothing in the file counts levels, and no cap is passed in from the public entry point readTable() at line 252.

list_two.title: A four-byte length off the wire sizes the byte array before any content is read
list_two.impact: A peer that spends four bytes makes the decoding process commit up to ~2 GiB of heap before it can fail. readFully() then throws EOFException, but the array already exists; repeated across frames or connections this is OutOfMemoryError or sustained GC pressure in the application embedding the library, with no data or credential needed by the sender. The same line also converts an over-large length into UnsupportedOperationException — an unchecked exception on a decode path whose callers are declared to throw IOException, so it escapes protocol error handling instead of being reported as a malformed frame.

list_two.title: Shipped API source is generated from a build input the manifest never verifies
list_two.impact: Part of the published artifact's source is decided by a directory that is not in this repository and is not checked against anything — the spec is selected by file name and a version string, not by content. Whoever populates `deps/rabbitmq_codegen` in a build environment influences generated public API code without a reviewable change in this tree. No attacker path is claimed: this is the integrity of a build input, and it is recorded as one.
list_two.evidence:
pom.xml lines 110-112 declare the input outside the module:
    <deps.dir>${basedir}/deps</deps.dir>
    <codegen.dir>${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen</codegen.dir>
    <codegen.spec_version>0.9.1</codegen.spec_version>
Lines 613-636 run it at generate-sources through groovy-maven-plugin, goal `execute`, with `<script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script>` and `<spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json</spec>`, writing com/rabbitmq/client/AMQP.java and com/rabbitmq/client/impl/AMQImpl.java; lines 644-656 add that directory to the main source root with build-helper `add-source`. The comment at lines 102-108 says the directory should hold a working copy of another repository. Nothing in the manifest pins a commit or a digest, and no verification step precedes the execution.
